strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: decisive error recognition in multi-agent systems, where failures can cascade and debugging is expensive. The formalization of the earliest decisive error is clear and useful.

The motivation is well grounded: the authors analyze the Who&When dataset to show recurring failure structures and demonstrate that naive in-context learning degrades due to long trajectories and low signal-to-noise ratio.

CORRECT is a reasonable and practical framework: it combines offline error-schema extraction, online semantic retrieval, and dynamic cache management, and it avoids model retraining while using compact schemas for inference-time diagnosis.

The CORRECT-Error benchmark is a substantial contribution in scale and diversity: over 2,000 trajectories across seven task families, built with an error-injection pipeline seeded by human annotations, and validated via a human study. It addresses a real scarcity of large-scale MAS failure-attribution data.

The experimental breadth is strong: evaluations span open- and closed-source models (Qwen, Llama, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek), multiple datasets, and several baselines including LLM-as-a-judge, fine-tuning, and naive ICL.

The ablations are informative in intent: they examine schema-cache size, number of retrieved schemas, cross-dataset schema transfer, model upgrades, and an oracle-schema upper bound, which helps characterize when the method works.

The paper includes partial reproducibility details: appendix prompts for schema generation and schema-guided diagnosis, model hosting details, embedding model choice, RoPE/YaRN scaling, and masking of each trajectory to avoid direct self-schema leakage.

The reported gains are consistent in direction across many settings, e.g., on Who&When GPT-5 + CORRECT raises human-crafted Acc@0 from 8.6% to 17.2%, and on CORRECT-Error it raises several Acc@5 scores to the 90%+ range.
weaknesses: The central claim of narrowing the gap to human-level error recognition is not supported by evidence. No human step-level accuracy or human ceiling is reported on the same task, even though human disagreement is described as exceeding 50% in Who&When; this makes the abstract claim speculative.

The human-alignment validation of CORRECT-Error is internally inconsistent and under-specified. The text reports 47.1% synthetic misclassified as human and 42.3% genuine correctly identified, while the figure appears to show different values; the claim that 94.4% of synthetic trajectories were judged genuine by at least two of three labelers conflicts with a per-labeler misclassification rate near 47%. Sample size, labeler instructions, expertise, compensation, and statistical uncertainty are not reported.

Baseline coverage and fairness are weak. Fine-tuning is only shown for Qwen-2.5-7B on Who&When, with no hyperparameters, splits, or training details, and its exact-step accuracy is the same as zero-shot in the table (3.5%). CORRECT-Error experiments omit fine-tuned and ICL baselines entirely, and no stronger retrieval or chunked-trajectory ICL baseline is considered, so the comparison to naive ICL may be a strawman.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Although the paper reports averages over five runs, it provides no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several claimed improvements are small (e.g., GAIA 28.6 to 30.6), and the headline 'up to 20 points' gain depends on one model/dataset combination.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Key thresholds such as delta and theta_hot are not specified, cache initialization requirements are unclear, and there is no code or dataset release link. Schema generation uses GPT-5 with over 3 billion tokens, so the system is not 'near-zero overhead' in total cost; only inference overhead is claimed, and even that is not measured.

The 'training-free' and 'data-efficient' framing is overstated. CORRECT still requires annotated error trajectories or ground-truth labels to build and expand the schema cache, and the dynamic expansion relies on user feedback plus ground truth, which may be unavailable or noisy in real deployments.

The method does not address whether a trajectory has failed in the first place. It assumes a failed trajectory is given and localizes among failures, with no false-positive analysis on successful trajectories. This limits practical deployment claims for monitoring and reliability.

Potential circularity and leakage are not adequately discussed. CORRECT-Error is synthesized using GPT-4o-mini/GPT-5-nano, schemas are generated by GPT-5, and evaluation partly uses GPT-family models; this may favor schema-based diagnosis. Masking only each trajectory's own schema does not rule out broader distribution overlap between synthetic errors and schema-generation prompts.

Novelty is moderate. Schema-guided retrieval and cache-based knowledge transfer are incremental over retrieval-augmented prompting and prior LLM-as-a-judge failure-attribution work; the 'first' claims are overbroad. The main novel artifact is the dataset, but its validation has the issues above.

Presentation needs substantial improvement. Algorithm 1 is malformed, there are typos and naming inconsistencies ('BAAI-BPE-M3' should likely be BGE-M3, 'Correct' vs CORRECT, 'Handcrafted' vs Human-Crafted), table rows are merged confusingly, and some figure captions/numbers do not align with the main tables.

There is no explicit limitations section. Given the synthetic dataset, reliance on proprietary models, and unresolved human-alignment questions, an honest limitations discussion is needed before others can reliably build on the benchmark and method.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: step-level decisive error recognition in multi-agent systems, which is critical for debugging and reliable deployment.
Proposes a training-free, retrieval-based schema framework that avoids fine-tuning and can adapt online; the high-level idea of distilling reusable error schemata is promising.
Introduces CORRECT-Error, a large-scale synthetic benchmark with over 2,000 trajectories and a human evaluation study, helping address the scarcity of MAS error-attribution benchmarks.
Reports consistent improvements over baselines across several models and datasets, with some substantial gains on CORRECT-Error (e.g., Math500 +46.9 at Acc@1, HotpotQA +26.1).
Includes useful ablation studies on cache size, number of retrieved schemas, schema transfer, and schema-generator model upgrades.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter tuning is performed on the same datasets used for evaluation. The number of schemas k is chosen using Qwen-2.5-7B on Who&When and HotpotQA (the evaluation sets), with no validation split, which leaks test information and undermines the reported gains.

Human evaluation is internally inconsistent: the text says 47.1% of synthetic trajectories were misclassified as human, but also that 94.4% of synthetic trajectories were judged genuine by at least two of three labelers. These cannot both be true. Figure 5/12 numbers also do not align with the text, and the study validates only trajectory realism, not whether the injected error is the decisive/natural error.

Numerical results are inconsistent. In Table 2, the reported average improvements (+27.6 and +28.7 for GPT-4o-mini Acc@3/Acc@5) do not match the averages computed from the listed per-dataset numbers (~26.9 and ~26.8); the GPT-5-Nano section also has mismatches. This weakens confidence in the central results.

No statistical rigor: no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, despite small Who&When subsets where a 1.7% difference equals a single trajectory. Many claimed improvements may be noise.

Baselines are weak or insufficiently described. There is no comparison to recent failure-attribution methods such as Ge et al. (2025); the fine-tuning baseline lacks training details and may be a strawman; naive ICL is an acknowledged weak baseline; and the strongest LLM-as-a-judge variant is not consistently used.

Method and algorithm are under-specified. Algorithm 1 contains broken notation and unclear logic (e.g., {S'1}i=1, using ground truth label from data after user confirmation, replaying without specifying ground truth availability). Thresholds δ and θ_hot are not reported, and clustering/filtering/distillation procedures are not reproducible.

Efficiency claims are unsupported. Near-zero overhead and subseconds are not backed by latency, token, memory, or cost measurements. Offline schema generation uses GPT-5 and over 3 billion tokens, which is expensive and contradicts cheap/low-cost and lightweight claims.

Reproducibility is poor: no code or dataset release statement, no exact model versions, no full online-detection prompts, no handling of >32K-token trajectories for baselines or CORRECT, and insufficient details on human evaluation (sample size, instructions, IRB/consent, compensation).

Dataset validity is limited: CORRECT-Error is generated by injecting errors with GPT-5/GPT-4o, which may produce artificial, localized failures that do not match natural cascading MAS failures. Human validation checks realism only; it does not verify that the injected step is actually the earliest decisive error, nor does it measure annotation agreement on error location.

Generalization and transfer claims are overbroad. Transfer is only tested from human-crafted to algorithm-generated data; there is no real-world MAS deployment evaluation. The 104% of oracle result in Figure 10 contradicts the claim that oracle is an upper bound.

Presentation is poor: many typos and naming inconsistencies (CORRECT-ERROR vs. CORRECT-Error, Hand-Crafted vs. Human-Crafted, BPE-M3 vs. BGE-M3), broken sentences in §3.1, garbled algorithm formatting, and inconsistent figure/text references.
No limitations or ethics discussion. The paper does not discuss synthetic-data bias, potential misuse, cost/accessibility, failure cases, or negative societal impact.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: decisive error recognition in multi-agent systems, with a clear formalization and practical motivation for debugging, safe upgrades, and monitoring.

Proposes a lightweight, training-free schema-guided framework that avoids fine-tuning and the context-length/noise problems of naive in-context learning; the high-level design is intuitive and plausible.

Introduces CORRECT-Error, a large-scale (>2,000 trajectories) step-level annotated benchmark spanning seven task domains, which could be a useful resource for the community if properly validated and released.

Reports experiments across multiple model families and scales (Qwen, Llama, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek), with ablations on cache size, number of retrieved schemas, oracle schemas, cross-dataset transfer, and model upgrades.
Shows consistent improvements on the synthetic CORRECT-Error benchmark and some gains on the human-crafted Who&When subset, especially with GPT-5.
Includes an insightful analysis suggesting LLMs have limited ability to recognize their own errors during execution, reinforcing the need for external detection mechanisms.
The paper is generally well organized and the motivation figures (trajectory length, semantic similarity, naive ICL degradation) effectively communicate the problem setting.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: the approach is essentially retrieval-augmented LLM prompting with LLM-generated error schemas plus cache management, rather than a fundamentally new learning or inference mechanism. The 'first' claims are overstated without a broader comparison to RAG and error-attribution literature.

The central claims of 'training-free,' 'data-efficient,' and 'near-zero overhead' are not well supported. Schema extraction requires annotated error trajectories and expensive GPT-5 calls; online cache expansion relies on user feedback/ground truth; and the paper mentions over 3 billion tokens used to construct the dataset, contradicting low-cost claims.
No quantitative overhead, latency, token-cost, or deployment-cost analysis is provided, despite abstract claims of 'subseconds' and 'near-zero overhead.'

The human validation of CORRECT-Error is insufficient and internally inconsistent. Labelers were asked to distinguish synthetic from human trajectories, not to verify step-level decisive error labels. Reported numbers are contradictory (e.g., 47.1% synthetic misclassified vs. 94.4% judged genuine by at least two labelers; 42.3% vs. 47.1% for genuine trajectories).

The synthetic benchmark may not faithfully reflect real MAS failures: successful trajectories are generated and errors are injected by GPT models, with realism 'guided' only by a small human-annotated seed set. This limits claims about natural error distributions.

Absolute performance on the human-crafted Who&When benchmark remains low (e.g., GPT-5 + CORRECT reaches 17.2% exact-step accuracy and 37.8% within one step), and some CORRECT results are negative relative to the baseline (e.g., Gemini-2.5-pro on Algorithm-Generated Acc@0).
The paper claims to narrow the gap to human-level error recognition, but no human upper-bound baseline is reported. Human disagreement rates are mentioned but not used to calibrate the evaluation.

Main tables report no variance or confidence intervals despite stating five independent runs, and no statistical significance tests are provided. The fine-tuning baseline is limited to one model and may be under-tuned, making comparisons potentially unfair.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or dataset release link is provided; key hyperparameters (clustering method, similarity threshold δ, hot-cache threshold θ_hot, retrieval top-k, filtering/distillation rules) are unspecified; the appendix prompts are truncated; and the dynamic cache management process is not fully described.

The formal definition of a decisive error relies on counterfactual outcome verification, but the dataset labels are injection points or human annotations that are not validated against this definition. It is unclear whether the benchmark's ground truth truly satisfies the decisive-error criterion.
There is no limitations section. The paper does not discuss failure modes, dependence on user feedback, privacy/security risks, or ethical implications of synthetic error injection.

Some algorithmic descriptions are inconsistent: the text says one schema is generated per cluster, but Algorithm 1 loops over every annotated trajectory; dynamic management uses overlapping terms ('distill' vs. 'extract') and unclear feedback assumptions.
Evaluation setup details for Table 2 are unclear (which model is used as baseline, whether CORRECT uses the same base model, how schemas are sourced, and how many schemas are used per dataset).

strengths: Targets an important and under-addressed problem: decisive error localization in multi-agent LLM systems, where failures cascade and labels are expensive.
Proposes a simple, training-free retrieval/schema-based framework that avoids fine-tuning and can adapt online; the design is lightweight and easy to deploy in principle.
Introduces CORRECT-Error, a large synthetic benchmark (2,000+ trajectories across seven task families) built via an error-injection pipeline, with a human study attempting to validate realism.

Evaluates on both human-crafted Who&When and CORRECT-Error across many LLMs (Qwen, GPT, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek) and includes ablations on cache size, number of schemas, cross-domain transfer, retrieval noise, and hyperparameters.
Reports consistent improvements over LLM-as-a-judge, naive ICL, MIPRO, and a fine-tuning baseline, and provides a downstream intervention study showing targeted restart can improve success rates.
Includes a limitations section and impact statement, and the writing is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is weakened by the synthetic benchmark construction. Errors are injected by GPT-5, schemas are generated by GPT-5, and evaluation often uses GPT-5-family models, so the synthetic benchmark may be biased toward the same model's error patterns and schema style. The large gains on CORRECT-Error are therefore not strong evidence of real-world MAS error recognition.

The human-alignment study does not convincingly validate realism or decidiveness. The reported near-random classification (42.3% genuine correctly identified, 47.1% synthetic misclassified as genuine) could reflect labeler uncertainty or bias rather than indistinguishability; no inter-annotator agreement statistic, no test of whether injected errors preserve causal/decisive structure, and the text inconsistently refers to four vs. five labelers.

Potential data leakage and unclear experimental protocol. The paper does not clearly define train/test splits or specify whether cluster-level schemas for CORRECT-Error are generated from trajectories that are later evaluated. 'Masking each trajectory itself' is insufficient for cluster-level schema leakage. Online schema expansion/distillation also uses ground-truth labels ('Extract ground truth label from data' in Algorithm 1), which is not realistic in deployment and may leak test labels into the cache.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The abstract's code URL is blank, the dataset is only promised, and key details are missing: exact number of clusters and epsilon, schema counts per setting, prompt variants, embedding truncation budget, API cost accounting, and the human-study protocol. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported despite small evaluation sets; median over five runs alone is not enough.

On the real human-crafted Who&When benchmark, exact-step accuracy remains very low (max 17.2% for GPT-5 + CORRECT, 12.1% for Qwen-2.5-7B), and some CORRECT variants are negative at Acc@1. The claim of practical decisive error recognition and 'near-zero overhead' is therefore overstated; the downstream intervention improvement from 10% to 20% is still modest.

Methodological novelty is limited: the approach is essentially retrieval-augmented prompting with LLM-distilled error summaries and standard clustering/semantic search. The paper does not compare against simpler retrieval baselines (e.g., retrieved error summaries, human taxonomies such as MAST) or stronger fine-tuning baselines across model families, so the source of gains is not fully isolated.

Presentation has several inconsistencies and unsupported claims: 'up to 19.8%' vs 'up to 20 points', 'subseconds' latency without timing evidence, table/figure numbering and labeling issues, and an overly broad 'first' claim. The limitations section is honest but does not address the synthetic-data validity, label dependence, or potential leakage concerns.

strengths: Tackles a timely and important problem: decisive error attribution in multi-agent systems, where long, cascading trajectories make debugging costly.

Proposes a coherent, training-free pipeline (offline schema distillation, online retrieval, dynamic cache management) with a non-trivial set of ablations (cache size, number of retrieved schemas, oracle schema, retrieval noise, threshold sensitivity).
Introduces CORRECT-Error, a >2,000-trajectory benchmark with step-level annotations, which could be a useful community resource if its realism claims held up.
Includes an honest Limitations section acknowledging label subjectivity and the limitations of semantic-similarity retrieval.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracy is very low and undermines the central claim: best exact-step accuracy (Acc@0) is 12.1% (Qwen-2.5-7B) and 17.2% (GPT-5) on Human-Crafted Who&When. The headline 'up to 19.8%' is a single cell (GPT-5, Algorithm-Generated, Acc@0) and is not representative; on Human-Crafted the same model improves only +8.6. A 'decisive error recognition' system at ~12-17% exact accuracy is not obviously practically useful.

The claim of generalizing across 'seven diverse MAS applications' is misleading: the seven items (HotpotQA, Musique, WikiMQA, ARC, MMLU-Pro, Math500, GAIA) are task datasets executed by essentially one MAS (Magentic-One/AutoGen), not seven distinct applications or orchestration frameworks.

Potential contamination/leakage is not adequately ruled out. Schemata are distilled from ground-truth annotated trajectories, and the generation prompt (Fig. 9) explicitly requests 'Agent Name' and 'Step Number'. Retrieval is by trajectory similarity, so for near-duplicate trajectories the schema may directly leak the answer. Masking only the trajectory itself is insufficient given that the algorithm-generated split shows suspiciously high baselines and gains.

The 'training-free'/'data-efficient' framing is misleading. Building the cache requires annotated trajectories with error step and reason, and cache expansion relies on user feedback/ground-truth labels. The method is effectively retrieval-augmented ICL over labeled exemplars, so the data-efficiency advantage over fine-tuning is not established.

Evidence for CORRECT-Error's realism is weak and internally inconsistent. The human study reports near-random discrimination (47.1% / 42.3%) yet the text contradicts the confusion matrix (True Injected: 8.7 / 42.3; True Original: 1.9 / 47.1). The number of labelers is inconsistent (four in §4.2 vs. 'at least two out of five'), and 'at least two out of five' is described as 'strong inter-annotator agreement', which is not convincing.

Missing comparisons to the most relevant line of work: experience/memory-based agents and learning-from-experience methods (e.g., Reflexion, ExpeL) and other failure-attribution approaches. There is no dedicated related-work section covering these.

The fine-tuning baseline shows literally zero improvement (3.5 vs. 3.5 on Human-Crafted Acc@0), suggesting an under-tuned baseline, which weakens the argument that fine-tuning fails and inflates the perceived benefit of CORRECT.

Presentation problems: inconsistent terminology (schema/schema/template), numbers in text that do not match tables/figures (e.g., Fig. 5b reports 12 vs. Table 1's 12.1), a dense and error-prone table layout, and an abstract 'up to 19.8%' that is cherry-picked.
Reproducibility concerns: no code link despite 'publicly available', data only promised, and heavy reliance on proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5) for both schema generation and detection.

Metric interpretation is weak: Acc@5 with ±5-step tolerance produces very high numbers (e.g., HotpotQA 94.2%) that may not reflect actionable localization, and the large difficulty gap between Human-Crafted and Algorithm-Generated splits suggests the synthetic benchmark may be easier or partly leaky.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: decisive error recognition in multi-agent systems, motivated by concrete analysis showing >80% of Who&When failure trajectories have a semantically similar counterpart and that naive ICL degrades due to long, noisy logs.

Proposes a practical training-free framework: schema extraction, semantic clustering, retrieval, and dynamic cache management; it is model-agnostic, lightweight, and deployable online with reported low overhead (<3.5% latency, API cost $0.86 -> $0.89).

Broad empirical study: seven MAS datasets/applications, both Who&When and CORRECT-Error, many LLMs (Qwen, Llama, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek), multiple baselines (LLM-as-judge, fine-tuning, ICL, MIPRO), and extensive ablations on cache size, number of schemas, oracle guidance, retrieval noise, transfer, model upgrade, and intervention.

Introduces CORRECT-Error, a 2,000+ trajectory benchmark with a bootstrap error-injection pipeline, covering diverse tasks and validated with substantial human annotation effort; if released, this could be a useful community resource.

Reports meaningful relative gains in several settings, e.g., GPT-5 +19.8 Acc@0 on algorithm-generated Who&When and average +28.7 Acc@5 on CORRECT-Error, with gains across model families and tolerance levels.
Discusses limitations honestly, including label subjectivity, reliance on semantic similarity retrieval, and multi-error trajectory failure cases, which is appropriate for a difficult problem.
weaknesses: The main benchmark, CORRECT-Error, is synthetic and generated by LLMs from a pipeline related to the method's schema design; this creates potential circularity. Human validation is weak (near-chance: 47.1% synthetic misclassified as genuine, 42.3% genuine correctly identified) and checks realism/authenticity, not whether injected errors are truly decisive or match natural failure distributions.

Absolute exact-step accuracy remains low on human-crafted Who&When (best 17.2% Acc@0 and 32.3% Acc@1 for GPT-5+CORRECT), limiting practical utility for decisive error localization; relative improvements do not show the problem is solved.

Some reported CORRECT results are negative or mixed (e.g., Gemini-2.5-pro algorithm-generated Acc@0 -0.8; Gemini-2.5-flash Acc@1 -0.8), which conflicts with the claim of consistent improvements across settings.
Lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting despite median-over-five-runs; many gains on Who&When (fewer than 200 trajectories) may be within noise.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is blank/incomplete; the pipeline relies on proprietary GPT-5/GPT-4o models and 3B+ token generation; prompts are partially provided but not all raw seeds, human-eval protocol details, or exact replication artifacts.

There is an internal inconsistency about human evaluation: the main text says four independent expert labelers, while later it refers to 'at least two out of five labelers'; such details need correction.

Method novelty is incremental: LLM-generated schemata + semantic clustering + retrieval + cache management is close to retrieval-augmented generation, case-based reasoning, and experience replay; 'first schema-guided detector' is an overclaim.

The online cache management depends on user feedback or ground-truth labels to expand/refine schemata; the fallback to LLM-as-a-judge validation is mentioned but not experimentally evaluated, and realistic noisy/absent feedback settings are not tested.
The fine-tuning baseline is weak (3.5% Acc@0), and training details are only in the appendix; stronger or better-tuned fine-tuning baselines would make the comparison more convincing.

Presentation issues and typos remain: 'Magnetic-One' should be 'Magentic-One', 'BAAI-BPE-M3' likely should be 'BGE-M3', and several numerical claims in the abstract/intro are not consistently aligned with the tables.
